evidence: src/domain/entities/Project.ts: class Project with private constructor and static create() that trims name and throws ValidationError('Project name must not be empty')
src/domain/entities/User.ts: class User with the same pattern: static create() trims name and throws ValidationError('User name must not be empty')

src/domain/entities/Task.ts: class Task with static create(params: CreateTaskParams) that trims title and throws ValidationError('Task title must not be empty'); it uses the DueDate and TaskStatus value objects
src/domain/entities/Task.ts: markDone() checks currentStatus.isDone() and throws ConflictError, so the status-transition rule stays inside the entity
src/domain/entities/Task.ts: assignTo(userId) doc comment hands the user-existence rule to TaskAssignmentService, so that rule lives in one place and is not repeated in the entities
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The three files form one cohesive concern: domain entities. Each uses the same pattern: a private constructor, a static create() factory that validates, readonly identity fields, and errors raised through the shared DomainError types (ValidationError, ConflictError). Task uses the DueDate and TaskStatus value objects and changes its own state only through methods (markDone checks TaskStatus.isDone() before changing status). Project, Task and User all repeat the same check: trim the text and reject it if empty. But each check is a separate invariant for a different field (project name, task title, user name), and each error message is specific to that entity. This is a repeated coding style, not one rule copied into several places, so it doesn't meet the fail condition. Task.assignTo is public and its doc comment hands the 'user exists' check to TaskAssignmentService. That rule therefore lives in one place, the domain service, and no file in this unit bypasses it. It is a weakness in encapsulation, but it isn't a bypass by the module's own files. Overall, the module's abstractions are used consistently.
